title: CalyxBio - Model selection, context length, and tool-calling discovery
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment tradeoffs
summary: Initial scoping with CalyxBio to understand model-fit for genomics annotation pipelines. Customer needs long-context for full-read transcripts (~100k tokens in batches), multilingual support for research collaborators, and robust tool-calling (database lookups + lineage provenance). Discussed tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted for quick iteration, Dedicated for predictable throughput, and Private (VPC/on-prem) for data governance. Agreed to run a two-week bench: sample prompts, latency/cost spreadsheet, and an on-prem pilot scope for legal review.
next_steps: Redwood: share model comparison matrix + sample perf numbers (quantized vs fp16)
Customer: provide representative prompt set & 3 weeks of example sequences (anonymized)
Schedule: technical deep dive with Calyx infra + security (week of Apr 10)
Redwood: send SOC2 + KMS integration notes and draft pilot contract
action_items: Alex Thompson - Send model comparison spreadsheet and preliminary pricing - 2028-04-05
Jules Park - Upload anonymized prompt corpus to shared S3 bucket (link to be provided) - 2028-04-06
Priya Natarajan - Run tokenization and rough latency estimate for 32k/64k contexts on Mistral-32k variant - 2028-04-09
Sana Ibrahim - Share network/passwording constraints and firewall policy for VPC peering - 2028-04-08
transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-04-03 15:00 UTC | Duration: 54m
Attendees: Alex Thompson (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Dr. Mateo Ruiz (CTO, CalyxBio), Jules Park (ML Engineer), Sana Ibrahim (Head of DevOps)

[00:00] Alex Thompson: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Alex AE on the account, Priya is our solution engineer.
[00:10] Dr. Mateo Ruiz: Thanks, Alex. We appreciate it. Quick context from our side—CalyxBio builds annotation and transcription pipelines for sequencing labs. We're looking at adding an LLM layer for automated note summarization, literature linking, and a provenance tool that can call our internal database.
[00:26] Jules Park: Yep, and just to add, our major constraints: we often process long transcripts — whole-run reads — so context length is huge. Also multilingual: teams in Spain, Korea, and Brazil need native-level summarization.
[00:40] Priya Natarajan: Got it. On the Redwood side, we usually evaluate three levers: model architecture/variant (open models), deployment mode (hosted vs dedicated vs private), and runtime optimizations like quantization, batching and KV cache.
[00:53] Sana Ibrahim: For us governance is key. We may need an on-prem or VPC deployment because some of the raw reads can't leave our environment. SOC2 is fine, but the raw data residency rules are strict.
[01:05] Alex Thompson: Totally understand. We'll cover the private path and what that looks like — our Private offering can be on your VPC or on-prem appliance. Before that, curious — what success looks like for this project? Latency SLAs, throughput, cost targets?
[01:18] Dr. Mateo Ruiz: Success for phase one is high-quality summaries with <10% hallucinations on a curated eval set, 95th-percentile latency under 1.5s for short queries and under 10s for long-chunk processing, and predictable monthly unit cost. We'll tolerate slightly higher latency for batch long-run jobs.
[01:33] Jules Park: Also we want tool-calling to be reliable. For example, the LLM should call our provenance service to fetch experiment metadata and attach links in the summary. That means support for function-call style APIs or tool-calling hooks.
[01:44] Priya Natarajan: Redwood supports structured tool-calling and function-like calls — we do streaming and structured outputs. On the models side, what open models are you evaluating internally?
[01:54] Jules Park: We're looking at LlamaX-13B, Mistral-32k, and Falcon-40B variants — trying to balance cost and accuracy. LlamaX was good on small docs, but struggled with long context unless we do heavy chunking. Mistral-32k sounds promising because of native long-context.
[02:10] Alex Thompson: Right — a few notes there. Mistral-32k is great for native 32k contexts; we can run the 32k variant on Dedicated or Hosted depending on throughput. For 64k+ you typically need KV cache strategies and either model variants that support extended context or a chunking + retrieval approach. We have customers doing up to ~100k effective context by stitching KV cache and retrieval. That does add complexity to latency/cost.
[02:33] Dr. Mateo Ruiz: When you say KV cache stitching, is that something Redwood manages in the hosted mode?
[02:38] Priya Natarajan: Yes, in Hosted we provide automatic prefix caching and KV cache management where applicable — though for strict data residency you probably need Dedicated or Private so caching lives in your network. Also caching policies influence consistency, so we expose controls.
[02:51] Jules Park: On multilingual — we have datasets in Spanish, Korean, Portuguese. Which models do best? We've seen Mistral and Falcon produce decent outputs but tokenization sometimes breaks for Korean, causing token bloat.
[03:03] Priya Natarajan: Tokenization can be model-dependent. We recommend testing your actual payloads; we can run tokenization profiles as a quick step. For Korean, some models do better, and sometimes a subword tokenizer configuration helps. We'll run a small tokenization and perplexity pass as part of the bench.
[03:17] Alex Thompson: Also, if you need consistent deterministic outputs for downstream linking, we can suggest quantized FP16/INT8 profiles that trade a little quality for cost. Those profiles are available on Dedicated and Private with our Optimize toolkit.
[03:30] Sana Ibrahim: About tool-calling — how do you secure external calls? We need signed requests and end-to-end tracing so we can audit which model invocation triggered which DB call.
[03:41] Priya Natarajan: We have function-like tool calls that include metadata headers and trace IDs. For security, we can integrate with your KMS for signing tokens, and all calls go through dedicated logging — audit logs are retained per your retention policy. On Private, those logs can stay within your VPC.
[03:56] Dr. Mateo Ruiz: Good. Pricing — what's the delta between Hosted and Dedicated for sustained 24/7 inference?
[04:02] Alex Thompson: Hosted is usage-based; good for experimentation and variable workloads. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput and a commit that reduces per-token unit cost. We'll send a sample pricing sheet but ballpark: Dedicated becomes favorable at sustained high throughput — e.g., if you're doing continuous night-run batches and serving interactive queries, you likely cross the threshold.
[04:20] Jules Park: Another operational question — do you support A/B rollouts of model variants? We want to try Mistral-32k vs a quantized Falcon and monitor quality regressions.
[04:29] Priya Natarajan: Yes — our console supports canary rollouts and per-prompt eval hooks. We can wire your test prompts into a quality monitor and alert on hallucination rate and latency regressions.
[04:40] Dr. Mateo Ruiz: What's the onboarding for Private? Do you ship an appliance or installable package?
[04:46] Alex Thompson: Both options. For strict air-gapped environments we have an on-prem package; for VPC we provision a private control plane that talks to your endpoint, with customer-managed networking and KMS integration. The on-prem path takes longer due to security review and a small customization window.
[04:59] Sana Ibrahim: We'll need to run a legal review — specifically data retention and deletion guarantees. Also, KMS integration must support our HSM-backed keys.
[05:08] Priya Natarajan: Noted. We'll include our KMS/HSM integration notes in the packet and the SOC2 + ISO artifacts.
[05:15] Jules Park: For the bench, can Redwood run an initial baseline: 1) tokenization profile across our corpus; 2) latency on 8k/32k/64k contexts for Mistral/Falcon/LlamaX quant profiles; 3) a tool-calling reliability test hitting our mock provenance API?
[05:29] Alex Thompson: Yes — that's our standard bench. We'll need a sample prompt corpus (anonymized) and an endpoint for the mock provenance service (or Redwood can mock it to measure failure modes).
[05:41] Dr. Mateo Ruiz: We'll prepare the corpus and we prefer Redwood mock the provenance API for initial tests. Jules will upload the corpus.
[05:48] Jules Park: Yeah I'll put it in the shared space you create. One more gotcha — our pipeline sometimes pre-encodes chunks in custom tokenization for special primers; will that break your caching assumptions?
[05:59] Priya Natarajan: It can — custom pre-tokenization means we need to align cache keys to your encoding. We can work with your engineering team to version the cache keying scheme so staleness isn't an issue. That typically requires an SE-led dev session.
[06:15] Alex Thompson: Okay, let's recap the technical asks and next steps.
[06:19] Alex Thompson: Action items: Redwood will share a model comparison sheet and perf numbers, run tokenization/latency estimates for 8k/32k/64k on Mistral-32k and Falcon variants, and send SOC2/KMS docs. Calyx will provide anonymized prompt corpus and network constraints for VPC. We also schedule a deeper infra + security call next week.
[06:42] Dr. Mateo Ruiz: That sounds good. Any quick risks we should call out?
[06:46] Priya Natarajan: Main risk is the long-context cost and engineering effort if you want native 100k contexts. There's a clear engineering trade: do you want to pay for extended-context model variants or invest in retrieval+stitching architecture. We can model both in the bench.
[07:01] Jules Park: Also tokenization anomalies for Korean need to be verified — if token bloat is severe, cost will spike.
[07:07] Sana Ibrahim: And network egress for Hosted could be a blocker, so we need the legal and security review early.
[07:13] Alex Thompson: Great points. We'll prioritize the tokenization profile and egress/legal docs. Scheduling — does Apr 11 16:00 UTC work for a deep dive with your infra and legal folks?
[07:23] Dr. Mateo Ruiz: Apr 11 works. I'll invite our legal counsel.
[07:27] Alex Thompson: Perfect. We'll follow up with calendar invites and send the bench template. Thanks everyone.
[07:33] Dr. Mateo Ruiz: Thanks, appreciate it.
[07:35] Jules Park: Thanks.
[07:36] Sana Ibrahim: Bye.

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-hears: "KV cache" sometimes transcribed as "K V cash", "Mistral-32k" appears as "Mister 32k" in a few spots; speaker attribution may shift in auto-transcript.

References shared in call: model-comparison-sheet.xlsx (to be sent), SOC2-pack.pdf (Redwood), bench-template.csv (for latency/cost), mock-provenance-api-url (to be created by Redwood).
